candidate.answerReason: Divisibility by 5 forces S=5. Divisibility by 4 leaves QR=12,24,32. Applying the digit-sum test to RST eliminates the first and third cases and forces T=3 in the second, leaving P=1.

methods.label: Apply the divisibility tests
methods.explanation:
Start with the divisibility-by-\(5\) condition because it fixes a digit immediately. A multiple of \(5\) ends in \(0\) or \(5\), and \(0\) is unavailable, so \(S=5\).

Next, \(PQR=100P+(10Q+R)\). Since \(100P\) is divisible by \(4\), \(PQR\) is divisible by \(4\) exactly when its last two digits, \(QR\), form a multiple of \(4\). The digits \(Q\) and \(R\) are distinct members of \(1,2,3,4\). The last digit \(R\) must be even. Checking \(R=2\) gives \(QR=12\) or \(32\); checking \(R=4\) gives only \(QR=24\). Thus these three cases exhaust the possibilities.

A number is divisible by \(3\) exactly when its digit sum is divisible by \(3\). Apply this to \(RST\), whose digit sum is \(R+5+T\):

- If \(QR=12\), the remaining digits for \(P,T\) are \(3,4\). The possible sums are \(2+5+3=10\) and \(2+5+4=11\), so neither works.
- If \(QR=32\), the remaining digits are \(1,4\). The sums are \(8\) and \(11\), so neither works.
- If \(QR=24\), the remaining digits are \(1,3\). The sums are \(10\) and \(12\), so \(T=3\) and \(P=1\).

This gives \(PQRST=12453\). Indeed, \(124=4\cdot31\), \(245=5\cdot49\), and \(453=3\cdot151\), so every original condition holds. Therefore \(\boxed{P=1}\), choice \(\text{A}\).
